title: Check yourself: ordering and purity in predicate chains

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, which predicate should come first in an `and()` chain?

options.text: The costliest, most thorough check, so its verdict arrives early
options.says: The page says to order the chain from cheapest to most expensive, to get the most from short-circuiting.

options.text: Any of them, as the chain evaluates all of them regardless
options.says: The page says and() short-circuits, which is why the order of its parts matters.

options.text: The cheapest, most selective check, so later ones are skipped more
options.says: The page says to order predicates from cheapest to most expensive to maximize the short-circuit benefit.

questions.stem: Per this page, what goes wrong when a predicate given to a parallel stream's `filter` adds each element to a shared `ArrayList`?

options.text: Threads race on the list, so its contents can be lost or corrupted
options.says: The page calls a side effect inside a parallel filter a race condition and says to keep the predicate pure.

options.text: The list takes a lock on add, so the pipeline runs more slowly
options.says: An ArrayList takes no lock; the page names the result a race condition, not a slowdown.

options.text: Threads work on private copies, so the shared list stays empty
options.says: The list is shared, not copied; the page calls this a race condition.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: The cheapest and most selective check goes first in an and() chain, so the costly ones run least.
A Predicate should be pure, because a side effect inside a parallel filter races between threads.
